summary: Both occurrences are active, intransitive II Infectum in the glossary’s filing. The German emotion/result phrasing does not establish Detransitive morphology.

LuF 2/26 is already quoted as LuF 282/26 with an English shrieking translation. The supplied German instead describes panic; the discrepancy is retained as an editorial question, not resolved by rewriting either source.

At 113/84 the same form accompanies fear after seeing a body. It is compatible with the existing audible-cry sense, but the narrative supplies no independent test of silent startle. No new sense or quotation is added merely to lengthen the thin cell.
Does mṣarṣʕo necessarily denote a cry, or can it describe silent starting/shuddering? Compare both alarm contexts with the inherited vocal gloss.
Confirm the LuF 282/26 versus LuF 2/26 reference concordance and the basis of the inherited English shrieking rendering before changing the gloss or etymological discussion.
